text: A plumbing plan's compile failure counts as evidence only if a build could fix it (#733, refining D-0107 and D-0281). When an acceptance test's package doesn't compile on the base, the check runner stages a standard-library Go helper that type-checks the package's tests against compiled production exports, without running any initializer. The failure qualifies only if every error in the acceptance files is attributable to a production API a build may add or change: an undefined name or selector production can declare, or a relation the message names in which a production value, or a declared type naming a production type, takes part, where the test's own operands admit the operator. Unused imports and locals, syntax errors, test-local type errors, compiler directives and mixtures with valid API errors refuse the plan with the file and diagnostic. #730's first build failed on an unused import in its pinned tests, which no build could fix. Where attribution is uncertain the rule leans to accepting, since a wrongly accepted error is the older behavior while a wrong refusal blocks a valid plan, and a refusal tells the planner to state the expected type where the test receives the production value, a form the check always attributes. The build spent its two repairs with review findings open, so it was finished by hand to save Codex credits, after an independent review; the real-image budget check passed at 1,182 s for two concurrent cold runs and 1,239 s for three.
